metadata.note: Three historical railroads that connected Buffalo, NY to Niagara Falls, researched from Wikipedia and railroad-history sites in response to a question about whether there was a train from Buffalo to Niagara Falls in 1900 (yes -- there were three). The New York Central's Niagara Falls Branch (originally the Buffalo and Niagara Falls Railroad, running 1845, leased to NYC 1853) and the Erie Railroad's competing Suspension Bridge line (1868) were the two main steam railroads serving the falls; both lost their passenger service by the early 1960s, leaving Niagara Falls with no passenger rail at all until Amtrak returned Oct 29 1978 (see data/amtrak.geojson's Maple Leaf, amtrak-68, which is this same corridor's modern continuation, renamed Maple Leaf in 1981). Separately, the Buffalo and Niagara Falls Electric Railway (1895) was a pioneering, immensely profitable electric interurban powered by Niagara's own new hydroelectric plants; it became part of the International Railway Company in 1902 and ran until 1922. All three predate any GTFS/live-data era and have no modern segment of their own. Route geometry follows the real intermediate towns each railroad's own history describes, but is a simplified handful of waypoints, not surveyed track centerline. Era boundaries follow real corporate-history milestones (line openings, mergers, discontinuation dates); headway_min and avg_speed_kmh within each era are estimates, not sourced from real timetables.
metadata.source: Wikipedia, american-rails.com, niagarafallsinfo.com, ethw.org, cptdb.ca (see conversation for citations)
metadata.rule4_split_2026_08_24: Rule 4 ownership split. The Erie Railroad and the Delaware, Lackawanna & Western did not become one another -- they merged on October 17 1960 into a new company, the Erie Lackawanna Railroad (reorganized as the Erie Lackawanna Railway in 1968 under the Dereco holding company, and folded into Conrail April 1 1976). Before this pass the post-1960 years were still drawn in the predecessors' own colours, so one company appeared on the map in two different colours -- ex-Erie segments in Erie black #22223B, ex-Lackawanna in DL&W brown #7F5539. Every feature whose segments ran past 1960 has been split at the merger date into a second feature with identical geometry, company 'Erie Lackawanna Railroad', colour #A02C5A. Six features across six files: erie-mainline-jerseycity-buffalo, dlw-hoboken-scranton-buffalo, erie-salamanca-jamestown-dayton, erie-chicago-extension, erie-buffalo-niagara-falls, cmv-cleveland-youngstown. The NYS&W (nysw-jerseycity-stroudsburg) is deliberately NOT included -- it had reverted to independent operation by 1940 and was not part of the merger.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.interurban_audit: 2026-08-24: features on this layer that are inter-city electric railways were retagged mode='interurban' (previously 'streetcar' or 'intercity_rail') so the map can draw them distinctly from city streetcars and from steam roads. See CLAUDE.md Rule 7.

properties.line: Buffalo and Niagara Falls Electric Railway: Buffalo – Niagara Falls

segments.note: The Buffalo and Niagara Falls Electric Railway opened in 1895, running via Tonawanda; the roughly two-hour trip cost 35 cents one-way, with cars running up to 30 mph. Power was drawn from Niagara Falls' new hydroelectric plants over Tesla/Westinghouse AC transmission lines, and it became the most successful and profitable electric interurban in the US. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
